newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Two cosmonauts, back on Earth, reunited with wives.
newsitem.headline: Two cosmonauts, back on Earth, reunited with wives.

text.p: Two Russian cosmonauts landed safely on Earth on Thursday after one of the toughest missions in the history of manned space flight and flew to Moscow where they were reunited with their families.

Their blackened Soyuz capsule, dangling beneath a huge white and yellow brake parachute, floated smoothly down to the barren steppeland of Kazakhstan shortly before 4:20 p.m. Moscow time (1220 GMT), slightly behind schedule.
Commander Vasily Tsibliyev, 43, and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39, looked tired but well. They smiled broadly as they were escorted from the capsule into the blazing Kazakh sunlight.
Tsibliyev, who seemed to be the more animated of the two, said he felt "happy to be back on Earth."

The pair later flew to Moscow, feasting on the way on caviar, water melon, boiled potatoes and cucumbers, and were cheered by colleagues and relatives when they emerged from the plane at an airport just outside the city.
They embraced their wives and were showered with flowers. Tsibliyev's eldest daughter broke down in tears at seeing her father safe and sound.
The cosmonauts endured a series of major setbacks after arriving on board the space station Mir in February. The most serious was a June 25 collision between the station and its supply ship.
Mir has run on partial power since then. They also had to contend with a fire and a series of problems with their life support systems.
Helicopters bearing rescue teams clattered to the remote Kazakh site as soon as Soyuz landed. The two men gulped down water and doctors carried out medical checks.
There had been some concern about the health of Tsibliyev, who developed a stress-related cardiac problem while on Mir.
"Tsibliyev is in good condition. There is nothing out of the ordinary," said Igor Goncharov, the mission's head doctor.

The cosmonauts were flown by helicopter to the town of Dzhezkazgan where they had further tests, signed autographs for Mission Control officials and, with support, greeted local people who presented them with Kazakh hats and costumes.
"The cosmonauts are back...We are fully satisfied with their condition," Yuri Glaskov, deputy director of the Star City cosmonauts' training centre, told reporters in Dzhezkazgan.
Asked about the many problems on Mir during the two Russians' six-month stay, Glaskov said: "We will talk to them about this later and will sort it all out."
At Mission Control near Moscow, deputy fight director Viktor Blagov suggested that Tsibliyev would have some hard questions to answer in due course about the June 25 collision.

"We have found not a single fault in the systems of either Mir or Progress (the supply ship) during the collision. A logical conclusion follows -- technology was not at fault," Blagov told a news conference.
Blagov, signalling a breakthrough, said the new crew on Mir had managed to repair its faulty Elektron oxygen generating system but had not tried to start it yet.
President Boris Yeltsin said last week human error might have been to blame for the collision, which threatened Mir's future.
He sent a message of thanks on Thursday to the two cosmonauts, praising the "persistence, courage and heroism they showed during their mission."
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin left British-born Michael Foale and their two Russian replacements, Commander Anatoly Solovyov and engineer Pavel Vinogradov, on board Mir.
"I hope that everything bad that we've had will leave with us," Tsibliyev said earlier in a live broadcast from Mir. "We are leaving. See you on Earth."
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin were due to spend the night at the Star City training centre outside Moscow. They were likely to stay there for a week to 10 days before going home.
